bib.title: Random Forests (Chapter 15, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed.)

question: How do random forests reduce the variance of bagged trees by de-correlation, how are they used in practice, and how do they compare with boosting?
contributions: Defines random forests (Algorithm 15.1), covers OOB, variable importance, proximity plots, overfitting, and analyses variance, bias and the adaptive nearest neighbour view.

results.setup: Spam data, test set of 1536; boosting uses 5-node trees, 2500 trees chosen by 10-fold CV (Fig 15.1). Authors say RF is not significantly worse than boosting.

results.claim: The weaker GBM (depth 4) beats the best RF (m=6) at 1000 trees, Wilcoxon p=0.007.

results.claim: On nested spheres boosting easily beats random forests; smaller m is better for RF.
results.setup: 50 simulations, nested spheres in R^10, training size 2000, test 10,000; RF 500 trees (randomForest 4.5-11), GBM shrinkage 0.05, 2000 trees (gbm 1.5) (Fig 15.2 and footnote 3).
results.quote: Boosting easily outperforms random forests here.

results.claim: Pairwise correlation between bootstrapped trees is typically 0.05 or lower; between bootstrapped sample means about 50%.
results.setup: See Fig 15.9 (boxplots, 600 prediction points, simulation model 15.8).

Variance of average of B identically distributed variables with pairwise correlation rho is rho sigma^2 + (1-rho)/B sigma^2.
results.setup: Eq 15.1; limits benefit of averaging, motivates decorrelation.

limits: Comparisons with boosting rest on a few datasets (spam, California housing, simulations); boosting wins on nested spheres and California housing.
Bias/variance simulations use one additive linear model (15.8) and note patterns differ with model structure.
Proximity plots look similar regardless of data, casting doubt on utility (p.595).
Permutation importance does not measure effect of removing a variable, since surrogates would be used (p.593).
Software details (randomForest 4.5-11, gbm 1.5) are dated; 2008 licensing note on Salford Systems.
practices: Use m = floor(sqrt p), min node size 1 for classification; m = floor(p/3), min node size 5 for regression, but treat as tuning parameters (p.592).
Use OOB error as built-in cross-validation and stop adding trees once it stabilises (p.593).
Growing fully grown trees seldom costs much and removes one tuning parameter; increasing B does not overfit (p.596).
With many noise variables and few relevant ones, avoid small m (p.596).
Random forests need very little tuning (p.590).
